newsitem.title: CHINA: Deng's reforms are double-edged sword.
newsitem.headline: Deng's reforms are double-edged sword.

text.p: Deng Xiaoping's reforms unsheathed the double-edged sword of rising incomes and galloping inflation but many Chinese said on Saturday they were much better off than in the pre-Deng era.
Deng, whose 18-year rule ended on Wednesday night with his death at 92, created unprecedented opportunities for making money after the leftist excesses of his predecessor Mao Zedong.
"Mao made the Chinese stand up but Deng made us rich," said Yang Baisong, a 41-year-old taxi driver in Beijing.
"I can make 8-9,000 yuan ($960-$1,080) a month," Yang said. "That's pretty good and this car is my own."
Ren Biao, a bassoonist with China's Central Orchestra, managed to tuck away close to 100,000 yuan doing saxophone gigs at bars and hotels in Zhuhai, in southern Guangdong province.
Now with China's premier philharmonic, he draws a salary of about 2,000 yuan a month, the best of any troupe.
"But I also have to rehearse eight hours a day, every day, while other orchestras only practise every so often while they still draw salaries," Ren said.
Although Yang's and Ren's earnings are well above the 1996 average annual urban income of 4,380 yuan, even average workers say they are better off then they were 10 years ago.

"We have a television, a radio and refrigerator," said a car repairman in Dalian in northeastern Liaoning province whose salary before was just a few hundred yuan a month. "Things are only getting better."
Market-oriented agricultural reforms gave farmers the incentive to grow more, boosting rural incomes to an average 1,900 yuan ($230) for rural residents.
Fast food outlets such as U.S. giant McDonald's are doing brisk business despite prices that are a hefty fraction of an average worker's monthly salary.
Cell phones, pagers and Pierre Cardin clothes abound in affluent cities such as Beijing.
"Deng was a great man, people will miss him and appreciate him for greatly improving their living standards in such a short time," a retired factory worker said.
Yet Deng's reforms allowing private enterprise and the abandonment of central planning unleashed demons such as galloping inflation.
"I remember when two fen (one quarter of a U.S. cent) would buy a handful of candy or an ice lolly," said one 27-year-old housewife. "Now things cost several yuan."
Controlling price rises was one of the demands of the 1989 student-led protests centred on Beijing's Tiananmen Square that Deng ordered crushed by the army that June.
But China held its once troublesome inflation rate to a shade over six percent last year, down from 14 percent in 1995, while notching up economic growth of 9.7 percent.
